yarn-dinkum.meaning: Every paragraph and point survives, in order: "I didn't mean I wanted to buy Cambridge", "there's no lift in the building", "they'll swap the talent for a gold brick and lose the napkin", "Baron Munchausen was the first commercial traveller". The one change is currency: "with eight quid every Saturday night" and "he never gets more than sixty cents out of any quid", which moves a Chicago letter into pounds and makes the 106-cents arithmetic odd.
yarn-dinkum.sense: Terms fit: "a no-hoper steer" for the scalawag steer, "making a mug of yourself", "the old man's loaded and can wear it", "won't be a skerrick of real use". "a beaut education" strains a little for 'a good education', and "a quid's worth one hundred and six cents" mixes pounds and cents.
yarn-dinkum.authenticity: Natural Australian idiom used in place: "I've kept my trap shut about this till now", "your own nous", "send you broke", "dead careful", "heaps of room at the top". Only "beaut education" and the quid/cents mix read as forced.
yarn-dinkum.register: A steady level-3 retelling: the sentences are the original's, voiced with "cos", "bloke", "uni", "fair makes a bloke's shoulders hunch up". No swearing, within the dad allowance.
yarn-dinkum.tone: The dry, wry paternal lecture survives: "There's heaps of room at the top here, but there's no lift in the building" and "they generally don't lie in that particular way" keep the original's deadpan.
yarn-dinkum.flow: Reads easily aloud: "I can't hand you success on a plate. It'd do you no good, and it'd do the firm harm." The close stumbles on "the first commercial traveller, and my commercial travellers' bills".
yarn-dinkum.variety: Varied: "trap shut", "nous", "mug", "loaded", "wear it", "skerrick", "sweet-talk". "bloke" recurs often ("a bloke's shoulders", "young blokes", "a bloke gets rich", "the bloke who hasn't got one").
yarn-dinkum.essence: Unmistakably the merchant's letter, with its homely business similes intact: "feeding a no-hoper steer its own weight in corn when it won't fatten up" and "set up in the drapery business in a small way".

yarn-deadset.meaning: Close to the original throughout: "I didn't mean I wanted to buy Cambridge", "there's no lift in the building", "Baron Munchausen was the first commercial traveller". The steer line garbles: "feeding a no-hoper steer that won't fatten up its own weight in corn" makes the steer fail to fatten up its weight in corn. Currency moved to "eight quid".
yarn-deadset.sense: Most terms fit ("making a mug of yourself", "loaded and can wear it", "send you broke"), but "your ideas ... have got a bit big for their boots" puts a person-idiom on ideas, and "a quid is worth one hundred and six cents" mixes currencies.
yarn-deadset.authenticity: Natural where it is Aussie: "your own nous", "dead careful", "the old man's loaded". Some original phrasing left stiff: "I've got pride enough to believe", "by turning around the order the Lord laid down".
yarn-deadset.register: Level 3: the original's sentences with a moderate Aussie layer ("bloke", "uni", "young fellas", "beaut"). No swearing, which the dad allowance permits.
yarn-deadset.tone: Keeps the measured, dry fatherly tone: "There's plenty of room at the top here, but there's no lift in the building."
yarn-deadset.flow: Mostly smooth, but the misplaced clause "a no-hoper steer that won't fatten up its own weight in corn" and "the first commercial traveller, and my commercial travellers' bills" catch the ear.
yarn-deadset.variety: A fair spread ("nous", "mug", "loaded", "beaut", "big for their boots"), with "bloke" leaned on: "a bloke hunch", "young blokes", "a bloke can get rich", "the bloke who hasn't got one".
yarn-deadset.essence: Plainly the original letter, its similes and order kept: "they'd swap the talent for a gold brick and lose the napkin".

unharnessed.meaning: Everything is there, and it keeps the currency right: "with eight dollars every Saturday night", "sixty cents out of any dollar". "I didn't mean I wanted to buy Cambridge outright" adds only colour. The steer simile is reordered, "feeding a mongrel steer that won't fatten up its own weight in corn", which blurs it slightly.
unharnessed.sense: Terms fit their places: "making a galah of yourself", "the old man's loaded and can wear it", "won't be a scrap of real use", "if your expense accounts aren't telling porkies", "my reps' bills". "a mongrel steer" fits the scalawag steer.
unharnessed.authenticity: Sounds like a real Australian: "Course, the bills won't send me broke", "I've kept me mouth shut", "it's enough to make a bloke go round-shouldered just looking at it", "telling porkies".
unharnessed.register: Level 3: the letter's sentences carried in an Aussie voice without piling on. No swearing, within the allowance.
unharnessed.tone: The deadpan wisdom survives: "There's plenty of room at the top here, but there's no lift in the building." and "they don't usually tell porkies in that particular direction".
unharnessed.flow: Smooth and spoken: "I can't hand you success ready-made. It'd do you no good, and it'd do the firm harm." Only the steer clause snags.
unharnessed.essence: Unmistakably the merchant's letter, its homely similes intact: "they'd swap the talent for a gold brick and lose the napkin".

engine.meaning: Mostly the original verbatim, but word swaps change things: "I am scared stiff your ideas" turns a polite hedge into fear; "It is all with the bloke" garbles "It is all with the man"; "he never spends the dollar" after "a quid is worth" mixes currencies; "the son of the old bloke".
engine.sense: Several terms take the wrong sense: "scared stiff" for the hedge 'I am afraid', "a beaut business man" for 'a good business man', "Baron Munchausen was the first travelling bloke" for the trade term traveling man, "very, dead careful".
engine.authenticity: Bolted on: "Bloody hell, I simply mention these things", "a bloody good deal like feeding his weight in corn", with US and period forms left in: "scalawag steer", "dry-goods business", "run an automobile", "my drummers' bills".
engine.register: Largely untranslated, with a few swapped words ("bloke", "uni", "quid", "lift"), so it falls short of level 3; the swearing ("Bloody hell") is within dad but lands arbitrarily.
engine.tone: The wry lecture mostly survives because the original text is kept, but "Bloody hell, I simply mention these things" jolts it into an outburst the letter never has.
engine.flow: Broken joins: "unless you are very, dead careful", "It is all with the bloke", "Bloody hell, I simply mention".
engine.variety: Leans on "bloke" for every man ("a bloke can get rich", "a bloke can start", "the old bloke", "the bloke who hasn't licked stamps", "travelling bloke"), and "beaut" twice.
engine.essence: Recognisably the original, since most of it is the original: "If you gave some fellows a talent wrapped in a napkin".

yarn-troppo.meaning: All the original's points are there, but it changes one and adds others: "He can't, and he won't wear it" contradicts the original's point that he can afford it but won't; "Eight quid. Not a lot, but it's a start." and "Ya take the stairs, same as every man and his dog." add commentary; currency moved to quid.
yarn-troppo.sense: Most terms fit ("making a mug of yourself", "rolling in it", "isn't worth a skerrick", "the creative so-and-sos" for padded expense claims). "live under the one roof" stretches the spending-earning metaphor; "a quid's worth one hundred and six cents" mixes currencies.
yarn-troppo.authenticity: Lively and mostly natural: "I've kept me trap shut", "quick smart", "every man and his dog", "Galahs, the lot of 'em". Some lines feel like added patter: "Here's the truth of it.", "you're not getting rich that way, sunshine".
yarn-troppo.register: Heavier than level 3: it adds asides and tags throughout ("Well.", "Dead, dead careful.", "son", "sunshine", "mind") pushing toward a yarn, though without swearing past dad.
yarn-troppo.tone: The father's voice becomes more garrulous and teasing ("Galahs, the lot of 'em.", "the creative so-and-sos"), which softens the dry, measured restraint of the original.
yarn-troppo.flow: Reads well aloud, but the fragments stack in places: "Dead, dead careful." "Eight quid. Not a lot, but it's a start."
yarn-troppo.variety: Highly varied: "quick smart", "rolling in it", "sunshine", "every man and his dog", "skerrick", "galahs", "so-and-sos".
yarn-troppo.essence: Recognisably the letter with its similes, but the added commentary loosens its compact shape: "Ya take the stairs, same as every man and his dog."

yarn-dinkum.quote: with eight quid every Saturday night
yarn-dinkum.original: with eight dollars every Saturday night
yarn-dinkum.why: Converts a Chicago wage to pounds; and then "sixty cents out of any quid" mixes currencies.

yarn-dinkum.quote: a quid's worth one hundred and six cents
yarn-dinkum.original: a dollar is worth one hundred and six cents
yarn-dinkum.why: A quid is not a hundred cents; the arithmetic of the aphorism goes slightly wrong.
"beaut" as a plain attributive for an education sounds forced.

yarn-dinkum.quote: the first commercial traveller, and my commercial travellers' bills
yarn-dinkum.original: the first traveling man, and my drummers' bills
yarn-dinkum.why: Repeats the same phrase where the original varies it.

yarn-deadset.quote: feeding a no-hoper steer that won't fatten up its own weight in corn
yarn-deadset.original: feeding his weight in corn to a scalawag steer that won't fat up
yarn-deadset.why: The reordering attaches 'its own weight in corn' to 'fatten up', garbling the simile.

yarn-deadset.quote: have got a bit big for their boots back East
yarn-deadset.original: have swelled up a little in the East
yarn-deadset.why: A person-idiom applied to ideas; strains.
Chicago wage converted to pounds; then "sixty cents out of any quid" mixes currencies.

yarn-deadset.quote: the first commercial traveller, and my commercial travellers' bills
yarn-deadset.original: the first traveling man, and my drummers' bills

unharnessed.original: feeding his weight in corn to a scalawag steer that won't fat up

engine.quote: unless you are very, dead careful
engine.original: unless you are very, very careful

engine.quote: Bloody hell, I simply mention these things because I am scared stiff
engine.original: I simply mention these things because I am afraid

engine.quote: It is all with the bloke.
engine.original: It is all with the man.

engine.quote: Baron Munchausen was the first travelling bloke, and my drummers' bills
engine.original: Baron Munchausen was the first traveling man, and my drummers' bills

engine.quote: a beaut business man, and he never spends the dollar
engine.original: a good business man, and he never spends the dollar

engine.quote: a scalawag steer that won't fat up
engine.original: a scalawag steer that won't fat up

yarn-troppo.original: he can stand it, because he won't stand it
yarn-troppo.why: The original says the old man could afford it but won't; 'He can't' changes the claim and contradicts 'the bills won't send me broke'.

yarn-troppo.original: with eight dollars every Saturday night

yarn-troppo.original: a dollar is worth one hundred and six cents

summaries.yarn-dinkum: A faithful, natural level-3 retelling that keeps the letter's dry humour; only the dollar-to-quid swap and a forced "beaut" grate.
summaries.yarn-deadset: A close, light-handed level-3 version that keeps the tone; one garbled simile and the quid/cents mix are its faults.
summaries.unharnessed: The most natural and accurate version: idiomatic, varied, keeps dollars, and keeps the dry wit; one clumsy simile.
summaries.engine: Mostly the original with mechanical word swaps, some of which break grammar or sense, and a bolted-on "Bloody hell".
summaries.yarn-troppo: Lively and varied, but heavier than the brief, with one changed claim and commentary that loosens the dry letter.
